text: Brinewatch is a single salt-stained dock and a tavern lamp. Gulls argue over the pilings. Mira Venn watches you from the Salt Lamp doorway.
I walk up and greet Mira.
Mira wipes her hands on her apron. Call me Aunt Salt if you want a tab, she says. The attic pallet is yours.
I ask the ferryman his name and whether he can take me out at dusk.
The ferryman taps the spare oar under the bench. Kell Reed, he says. Not after dark, and not by the well path.
I go to the brine-well and fish out the bright thing on the ledge.
Your hook lifts a seven-eyed copper token. The stamp on the face reads CANARY-BELL-7E. Salt-lung keeps the well-gas out of your throat.
I buy Mira a lemon and hand it over.
Mira pockets the lemon, marks the errand done, and pours you a thimble of something sour. That tab item is closed.
I ask about the singing last night.
Fog-neap, Mira says. The Tide Choir only sings on fog-neap nights. Weather, not a church.
I sit on the dock and wait.

Gray water slaps the pilings. A coil of line ticks against a cleat. Gulls trade the same three insults they used at dawn. No one new comes up the ladder. The Salt Lamp lamp stays lit because Mira never puts it out before second tide. You can smell pitch, wet rope, and yesterday's fry oil. The ferry sits low, empty, oar still under the bench. Nothing happens that you would bother to write down.

A cart of empty barrels rolls past and stops for no reason. The carter swears at a stuck wheel, frees it, and leaves a stripe of rust water on the planks. Wind turns the tavern sign one squeak and back. You count nine gulls, then eight, then nine again. The well rope knocks its hook. Dock talk nearby is about nets, not names. Time stretches without adding a fact you do not already have.

The slip goes from pewter to oil-slick green. A crate lid floats by, then a knot of bladderwrack. Someone dumps a bucket far up-dock; the splash reaches you two breaths later. Your oilskin sticks to your wrists. The empty flask is still empty. If there is a drowned bell in the well, it does not ring from here. This stretch of afternoon is weather and wood, not plot.

Second tide lifts the ferry a handspan and sets it down. Mira's door stays half-open on the same wedge of lemon-crate she has used for years. A boy runs past with a message that is not for you. The brine-well is out of sight behind the nets. Whatever you pulled from it earlier is not mentioned again in this dull hour. The village is a loop of small sounds, and the loop does not teach you anything new.
